reasoning_trace: The bar chart shows partial results on Aug 01 with Trail A at ~2300 votes, ahead of B (~1900) and C (~1700). They extrapolate the current leader in an incomplete tally to the final outcome, ignoring that the uncounted half of the votes (a pool larger than any current margin) could reverse the ordering. This is exactly the misleader CALVI builds into this item: presenting cherry-picked/incomplete data as if it were conclusive.
misconception: Treats a leader in partial/incomplete data as the guaranteed final outcome, ignoring that uncounted data could change the result.
short_label: Extrapolates partial tally to final outcome

key: In which season does each month have less rain than the month before? + table.png||Summer

reasoning_trace: In the table, Spring is the season where every month drops relative to the previous month (March 60, April 40, May 2, after February 75). Summer shows June 1, July 1, August 1: the lowest rainfall in the year, but flat, not decreasing. Many readers translate the question 'each month have less rain' into 'the season with the least rain', and Summer's string of 1s is visually the obvious minimum. This substitutes a simpler judgment (lowest values) for the asked comparison (each value lower than its predecessor). The high share of choosers, including able ones, fits how natural that substitution is.

reasoning_trace: Fall's months read September 10, October 25, November 55: each month has MORE rain than the month before, the exact mirror of the required pattern. A reader who flips the direction of the comparison, e.g. mentally checking 'each month less than the next' or scanning the column from bottom (November 55) upward to September 10, sees a consistently shrinking sequence and picks Fall. The table layout makes bottom-up scanning easy since Fall is the last block before the average row. This is a direction-of-comparison reversal rather than a failure to compare at all.
misconception: Reverses the direction of a sequential comparison, reading a consistently increasing series as decreasing (or scanning the table in reverse order).

Winter also holds the largest numbers in the table, which draws attention. With only 4 low-ability choosers, this looks like a partial check of one adjacent pair plus salience of the big values rather than a full month-by-month verification.

A reader who swaps one correct row for a near-miss, e.g. taking Tanith (14.1, literacy 28.7) or Ark (12.2, 35.4) in place of Myar (16.2, 83.2) or Debstam, drags the mean down several points toward 87.7. Because the table is unsorted, off-by-one errors in picking the fifth-largest spender are easy. The choosers' fairly high ability suggests genuine computation with one wrong row included.
misconception: Includes a wrong row when picking top-N from an unsorted table column, corrupting the computed average.

The interval Jun 2803 to Dec 2806 sits inside that first long, unbroken climb, so a reader who interprets 'highest increase in the trend' as 'when the trend was steadily/most consistently rising' selects it, even though its net change (+2.0) is the smallest of the rising intervals. The actual largest increase, +3.4, occurs in the final interval Jun 2810 to Nov 2813. This reads the question as about the character of the trend (sustained rise) rather than the magnitude of change between the interval's endpoints.
misconception: Judges 'largest increase' by how steady or unbroken the rise looks rather than by the magnitude of change between interval endpoints.

A reader anchoring on that within-interval spurt, or computing the relative (percentage) change, for which this interval is actually the largest (about 32%), lands here. key: Which of the following is true about the three brands of shampoo in city Y from 2001 to 2005? + T25.png||The market share of brand C is on an increasing trend from 2001 to 2005.
item_id: Which of the following is true about the three brands of shampoo in city Y from 2001 to 2005? + T25.png
wrong_answer: The market share of brand C is on an increasing trend from 2001 to 2005.
reasoning_trace: The x-axis of this 100% stacked bar chart is deliberately scrambled: the bars are ordered 2003, 2002, 2005, 2004, 2001. Brand C's (bottom, pale) share across the bars as drawn left-to-right reads about 25%, 42%, 45%, 48%, 55%, a clean monotonic rise. A reader who assumes, as is almost always true, that a year axis runs chronologically left to right sees C 'increasing from 2001 to 2005' without checking the tick labels. In true chronological order (2001: 55%, 2002: 42%, ...) C actually starts highest, so the correct statement is that C is higher in 2001 than 2002. The error is trusting conventional axis ordering over the printed labels.
misconception: Assumes a categorical/time axis is in chronological order and reads left-to-right position as time, ignoring the actual tick labels.

A reader assuming the leftmost bar is 2001 sees B's share there as clearly its largest across all bars and endorses the statement. In the true 2001 bar (rightmost), B is only about 33%, smaller than in 2003. So this answer is the same axis-order trap as the modal error, expressed through brand B: position is read as year without checking labels.
misconception: Assumes a categorical/time axis is in chronological order and reads left-to-right position as time, ignoring the actual tick labels.
short_label: Leftmost bar read as earliest year

This is the item's designed misleader: a mismatch between the question's time window and the data's window. Forty percent of participants, including able ones, generalized the visible flat segment to the whole 60-year period.
misconception: Extrapolates the trend of the plotted time window to a longer period the chart does not cover, ignoring axis range limits.

reasoning_trace: In this stacked area chart, Olivia is the bottom band (0 to ~4,700 in 2014) and Isla is the middle band (~4,700 to ~8,700), so both bands are about 4,000-4,700 thick and the true ratio is about 1 to 1. A reader who does not treat the layers as stacked instead reads each series at the height of its upper boundary: Olivia at ~4,700 and Isla at ~8,700. Comparing 4,700 to 8,700 gives almost exactly 1 to 2. This is the single most natural cumulative-position misread, which is why nearly half of respondents chose it.
misconception: Reads the top boundary of a stacked area layer as that series' absolute value instead of subtracting the layer below.
short_label: Cumulative boundary read as series value

reasoning_trace: This CALVI chart sorts the bars by rainfall amount, not by date: the x-axis reads Apr 28, May 06, May 03, May 07 ... A reader who assumes, as in a normal time series, that the left-to-right order is chronological sees a monotonic climb ending in the tallest bar and concludes that rainfall peaked 'at the end' of the 14 days. In fact the tallest bar is May 02, which falls in the first half of the Apr 27-May 10 window. Almost half of respondents chose this, exactly what the deceptive sorted ordering is designed to induce.
misconception: Assumes the left-to-right order of categorical axis labels is chronological without reading the labels, so a value-sorted chart is read as a temporal trend.

Having spot-checked only a few early dates, they compress 'the maximum occurs early' into 'rainfall peaked at the beginning,' even though the very first days (Apr 27-28: 75mm and 32mm) are not the peak. The correct, weaker statement that there was simply more rain at the beginning than the end gets passed over for this stronger but inexact claim.
misconception: After partially re-ordering scrambled time labels, treats a high value found early in the period as the peak occurring 'at the beginning' without checking all days.
short_label: Early high value equated with beginning peak

Angle estimation for pie slices is known to be error-prone, and the lung slice is the largest labeled slice, sitting beside a cluster of three small slices; contrast with those small slices inflates its apparent size. A reader eyeballing the blue wedge without anchoring it to the vertical and horizontal diameters judges it as 'about a third' of the circle and picks 33. The low ability of these choosers fits an unanchored visual estimate rather than a computed one.

A reader who mentally discards the 'other' half — treating the question as lung's share among the specifically named cancers — sees lung filling half of what remains and answers 50. This is a part-of-part normalization error: the percentage is computed relative to a visually salient subset rather than the whole pie.
misconception: Computes a category's percentage relative to the labeled subset of a chart rather than the whole, ignoring a residual 'other' category.

A reader who assumes the standard convention that up means more never checks the axis tick labels and reports the visual downward slope as a decreasing trend. Fully 71% of respondents, including high-ability ones, made this error — the inverted axis defeats the default reading.

With so few choosers and no single visual driver, this is best treated as residual uncertainty rather than a specific systematic misconception.

Either way the task's comparison operation was replaced by a magnitude judgment on the values themselves.

With only 6 choosers and no strong systematic pull, this is a subtraction/scanning slip more than a stable misconception.

A reader who evaluates the trend from the salient mid-period decline, or who compares the ending level to the mid-period peak instead of to the starting value, concludes there was no general increase. The question even warns about 'some variation,' and these 12 respondents let that variation dominate the start-to-end comparison.

misconception: Maximizes only the outcome axis of a scatterplot, ignoring the condition on the other axis in a two-criterion question.

key: True or False: Predatory species Z is more prevalent in NC than in AZ. + T10.png||True
item_id: True or False: Predatory species Z is more prevalent in NC than in AZ. + T10.png
reasoning_trace: The choropleth uses a red sequential palette, but the legend is inverted: the palest cream color is labeled 'Very High' and the deepest red is labeled 'Low'. On the map, NC is filled with a noticeably darker orange-red than AZ, which is a light orange. A participant glances at the two labeled states, sees NC is darker and more saturated than AZ, and applies the near-universal convention that darker color means a larger value, concluding NC has higher prevalence and answering 'True'. In fact, because dark means Low here, NC's darker fill indicates lower prevalence than AZ, making 'False' correct. The sizeable share choosing 'True' (about 22%) reflects readers who never checked the legend's direction.
misconception: Assumes darker/more saturated fills in a choropleth or heatmap always encode higher values, without verifying the legend's actual (possibly reversed) mapping of color to magnitude.
short_label: Darker color assumed to mean more

key: Which planet has the lowest adult literacy? + sp-table-8.png||Repler

The result is reporting the minimum of a partial scan rather than of the full column.
misconception: Finds an extremum by incomplete scanning of an unsorted table, anchoring on the last rows or forgetting early values.

A participant who judges the ratio directly from the drawn bar heights, without reading the axis labels, sees A as roughly half of B and answers 50%. The answer sits between the pure-visual and pure-numeric readings, which is characteristic of anchoring on the visual and adjusting insufficiently.

Alternatively, an exaggerated impression of the truncation effect ('the Aug 10 bar looks well under half') lands in the same place. The lower ability of these choosers fits a compounded misreading.

key: What is the number of concert tickets sold on Aug 10 as a proportion of that on Aug 11? + T3.png||20%

The relatively high ability of these choosers supports this: they extracted correct numbers but answered the wrong quantity.
misconception: Confuses 'A as a proportion of B' with the percentage difference between A and B, reporting (B-A)/B instead of A/B.

A participant who equates 'lies outside the relationship' with 'is the most extreme or most prominent point' picks Beijing, even though Beijing actually sits close to the high end of the trend. This confuses being an extreme value with deviating from the trend.

In fact Tokyo is roughly on the length-stations trend; only its bubble size (a third variable) is unusual. This conflates the size encoding or edge position with deviation from the x-y relationship.

key: About how much did the price of a barrel of oil fall from April to September in 2015? + item5.png||$45.00

A participant who traces to September and reports the price there, instead of subtracting it from April's price, answers $45. This is answering 'what was the price in September' rather than 'how much did it fall' - reporting an endpoint instead of computing the change. The low ability of these choosers fits failure at the two-step task.

key: About how much did the price of a barrel of oil fall from April to September in 2015? + item5.png||$17.00

Only 3 people, with high ability, chose this - consistent with a small reading or subtraction imprecision by people doing the correct operation.

key: Do U.S. states have a more similar number of windy days in the summer or in the winter? + T2.png||Winter
item_id: Do U.S. states have a more similar number of windy days in the summer or in the winter? + T2.png
reasoning_trace: The two choropleth maps use only three bins: Low (0-7), Intermediate (8-15), and an open-ended High (16+). In the winter map almost every state is the same dark 'High (16+)' color, while the summer map shows a mix of all three shades. Participants overwhelmingly (84%) concluded that states are more similar in winter because the winter map looks uniform. The trap is that '16+' is unbounded: states in that bin could have 16 or 60 windy days, so actual similarity cannot be inferred from the binned colors. This is the classic error of reading uniform color categories as uniform underlying values.
misconception: Treats uniform color within a binned choropleth category as evidence that the underlying values are similar, ignoring that bins (especially open-ended ones) hide within-bin variation.
short_label: Uniform bin color implies similar values

key: Do U.S. states have a more similar number of windy days in the summer or in the winter? + T2.png||Summer
item_id: Do U.S. states have a more similar number of windy days in the summer or in the winter? + T2.png
reasoning_trace: The summer map shows large regions sharing the pale 'Low (0-7)' color across the South and Northeast, so a participant focusing on those blocks of identical light color could judge summer as the more uniform season - the same binning fallacy as the 'Winter' answer but keyed to a different region of the map. Alternatively, with only 7 low-ability choosers, some may simply have swapped the two maps or guessed. Either way there is no valid inference available from three coarse bins; these participants still believed the binned colors could answer the similarity question.
misconception: Believes coarse binned color categories permit judgments about the similarity of underlying values, focusing on whichever map region looks most uniform.

key: True or False: If the temperature gets higher than 100°F, then the bottles of water sold must be greater than 750. + T46.png||Cannot be inferred / Inadequate Information

Choosing 'None of the above' requires wrongly rejecting that statement: the B (25%) and C (20%) slices are adjacent, similar in size and in similar green hues, so a reader comparing them by area alone (ignoring the printed percentages) can judge C bigger than B — which falsifies option 3 and also option 2, while A=55% falsifies option 1, leaving 'None'. The error is a slice-area misjudgment between two similar adjacent wedges.
misconception: Judges relative size of similar adjacent pie slices by area impression rather than the printed values, misordering close slices.

key: Which season has the most rain? + table.png||Summer
item_id: Which season has the most rain? + table.png
reasoning_trace: The table clearly shows Winter dominating (100+110+75=285 mm) while Summer months are 1, 1, and 1 mm. Answering Summer contradicts every number in the table, so these 3 low-ability responders were not reading the values at all: they most plausibly answered from a real-world prior that summer is the rainy season (true in many monsoon climates), or matched 'most' to a season name without consulting the data. Prior belief substituted for table lookup.
misconception: Answers from real-world prior beliefs about the domain instead of reading the values presented in the table or chart.

key: On how many planets does high expenditure per primary student seem to have a high positive impact on adult literacy? + sp-4.svg||3
item_id: On how many planets does high expenditure per primary student seem to have a high positive impact on adult literacy? + sp-4.svg
reasoning_trace: The scatterplot shows planets by expenditure per student (x) and adult literacy (y), with a clear high-high group (e.g., Exxor at roughly 23, 93) separated from a mid/low cluster (Alpeh ~58, Arden ~51, Burley ~43, Bryak ~35, Getorin ~29, Rhea ~25). Counting which planets sit in the high-expenditure AND high-literacy region requires the reader to set two informal thresholds. A participant who draws the 'high expenditure' cutoff slightly further right, or who demands a slightly higher literacy level, excludes one borderline planet that the answer key includes and counts 3 instead of 4. Their procedure is correct; only the placement of the subjective threshold differs by one point.
misconception: When counting points in a 'high on both variables' region of a scatterplot, places the subjective cutoff for 'high' slightly differently than intended and excludes a borderline point.

key: On how many planets does high expenditure per primary student seem to have a high positive impact on adult literacy? + sp-4.svg||5
item_id: On how many planets does high expenditure per primary student seem to have a high positive impact on adult literacy? + sp-4.svg
reasoning_trace: The task is to count planets where high spending co-occurs with high literacy. The chart has an ambiguous middle zone: Arden sits at moderately high expenditure (~13) with literacy just above 50, and Alpeh has high literacy (~58) at moderate spending (~9). A participant using a lenient definition of 'high' on one or both axes pulls one of these borderline planets into the count, arriving at 5 rather than 4. The mean ability of these choosers (~0.56) is relatively high, consistent with people doing the right two-axis counting task but with a looser inclusion criterion, not with random error.
misconception: When counting points that are 'high' on both scatterplot axes, uses a lenient cutoff and includes borderline moderate points in the high-high group.

key: On how many planets does high expenditure per primary student seem to have a high positive impact on adult literacy? + sp-4.svg||1
item_id: On how many planets does high expenditure per primary student seem to have a high positive impact on adult literacy? + sp-4.svg
reasoning_trace: In the visible plot, one planet (Exxor, ~23 on the x-axis with literacy above 90) stands dramatically apart from the pack; the remaining labeled planets cluster below 15 expenditure and below 60 literacy. A participant who interprets 'high expenditure with high positive impact' as only the extreme, visually isolated outlier counts just that single standout point and answers 1. This reflects treating 'high' as 'exceptional relative to everything else on the plot' rather than as a region containing several qualifying planets, so all other qualifying high-spend/high-literacy planets are dismissed as merely moderate. The lower mean ability of these choosers (~0.40) fits an overly coarse reading that latches onto the single most salient point.
misconception: Interprets 'high on both variables' as only the single most extreme, visually isolated point, ignoring other qualifying points.

key: On how many planets does high expenditure per primary student seem to have a high positive impact on adult literacy? + sp-4.svg||9
item_id: On how many planets does high expenditure per primary student seem to have a high positive impact on adult literacy? + sp-4.svg
reasoning_trace: The scatterplot as a whole has a loosely positive drift: planets that spend more tend to sit somewhat higher in literacy, with the extreme point Exxor anchoring the trend. A participant who reads the question as 'on how many planets does expenditure seem to positively affect literacy?' evaluates the global trend instead of counting points in the high-high quadrant, and concludes that the positive relationship holds for essentially all planets, answering 9 (all, or all but one exception that visibly bucks the trend, such as low-literacy Rhea or Getorin). This substitutes a judgment about the overall correlation for the required point-counting task.
misconception: Substitutes a judgment of the overall positive trend for counting points in a specific region, so nearly all points are counted as showing the effect.

key: On how many planets does high expenditure per primary student seem to have a high positive impact on adult literacy? + sp-4.svg||2
item_id: On how many planets does high expenditure per primary student seem to have a high positive impact on adult literacy? + sp-4.svg
reasoning_trace: The visible chart shows one unambiguous high-high planet (Exxor at ~23 expenditure, ~93 literacy) and a handful of planets at moderately high spending whose literacy hovers near or just above 50. A participant using a demanding literacy criterion (e.g., only literacy well above 60 counts as 'high impact') keeps Exxor plus a single companion in the qualifying region and rejects the two borderline planets the key counts, arriving at 2. Notably these choosers have the highest mean ability (~0.62), suggesting careful readers who applied a stricter but defensible definition of 'high' rather than a careless read. It is the same threshold-placement issue as the answer 3, just more severe.
misconception: Applies an overly strict definition of 'high' on one scatterplot axis, so borderline qualifying points are excluded from the count.

key: In which season does each month have less rain than the month before? + radial.png||Summer
item_id: In which season does each month have less rain than the month before? + radial.png
reasoning_trace: On the radial chart, summer's wedges (Jun 1, Jul 1, Aug 1) are almost invisible slivers at the center, while spring shows the actual monotone decline (Mar 60, Apr 40, May 2, each also below Feb's 75). Nearly 40% of participants chose Summer, which is far too systematic to be noise: readers see that summer has the least rain overall and equate 'least rain' with 'rain decreasing each month.' The tiny, roughly equal wedges cannot show a month-to-month decrease (the values are flat at ~1 mm), but the extreme smallness dominates the impression. The reader answers a magnitude question ('when is rain lowest?') instead of the asked trend question ('when does it decrease every month?').
misconception: Confuses low absolute values with a decreasing trend, answering where the quantity is smallest rather than where it declines month over month.

key: In which season does each month have less rain than the month before? + radial.png||Fall
item_id: In which season does each month have less rain than the month before? + radial.png
reasoning_trace: The radial chart lays months out clockwise starting from Dec at the top, so within Fall the correct temporal order is Sep (10) -> Oct (25) -> Nov (55), an increase. A participant unfamiliar with the chart's clockwise month ordering can scan the Fall quadrant in the opposite angular direction, reading Nov -> Oct -> Sep, and sees wedge radii shrinking 55 -> 25 -> 10, i.e., a perfect month-by-month decrease. Choosing Fall thus reflects traversing the polar layout in the wrong direction rather than misjudging the wedge sizes themselves; the sizes were read accurately but in reversed time order. This is a hazard specific to radial/polar time layouts where temporal direction is not marked.
misconception: Reads time in the wrong angular direction on a radial chart, so an increasing sequence is perceived as decreasing.
short_label: Reversed time direction on radial chart

key: In which season does each month have less rain than the month before? + radial.png||Winter
item_id: In which season does each month have less rain than the month before? + radial.png
reasoning_trace: Winter on this chart runs Dec (100) -> Jan (110) -> Feb (75): rain rises into January before dropping sharply. The Jan-to-Feb drop of 35 mm is the single largest month-to-month decrease on the chart and the winter wedges are the most visually dominant elements. A participant anchoring on that salient big decline can generalize it to the whole season, overlooking that Dec -> Jan actually increases. With only 4 choosers this is a minor pattern, but the pull is plausibly the salience of the large winter wedges and their prominent decline, i.e., verifying only part of the season's sequence.
misconception: Generalizes from one salient month-to-month change to the whole period without checking every step in the sequence.

key: What is the average adult literacy on the 5 planets that spend the most on primary students? + sp-7.svg||86.5
item_id: What is the average adult literacy on the 5 planets that spend the most on primary students? + sp-7.svg
reasoning_trace: The task requires identifying the 5 rightmost points (highest expenditure) and averaging their y-values. Among the visible high spenders, Rokanan (~87) and Locr (~77) are high in literacy, but Helicon (~10.2 expenditure, only ~25 literacy) also belongs in the top-5 spender set and drags the average down to 82.9. A participant who visually averages the top-spending group tends to anchor on the salient cluster of high points and underweight or drop the single low outlier Helicon, yielding a higher average of 86.5. These were the highest-ability choosers (~0.65), consistent with people who did the right selection but whose visual averaging discounted the outlier. This is the classic robust-impression bias in visual mean estimation.
misconception: When visually averaging a set of points, underweights or excludes a low outlier, biasing the estimated mean toward the majority cluster.

key: What is the average adult literacy on the 5 planets that spend the most on primary students? + sp-7.svg||90.1
item_id: What is the average adult literacy on the 5 planets that spend the most on primary students? + sp-7.svg
reasoning_trace: The question asks to select planets by expenditure (x-axis) and then average their literacy (y-axis). The chart's highest literacy values are Marvan (~90), Rokanan (~87), Locr (~77), and other high points; a participant who confuses the selection variable ranks planets by literacy instead of spending, picking the 5 highest points on the y-axis. Averaging those five high-literacy planets gives roughly 90, matching option 90.1. Notably Marvan spends only ~7.2, so it should not be in the top-5 spender set at all, but it is the most visually salient point (topmost) and gets included when 'the most' is applied to the wrong axis. This axis-role swap is a common failure on scatterplot filter-then-aggregate tasks.
misconception: Selects points by ranking on the wrong axis, filtering by the outcome variable instead of the stated selection variable.

key: What is the average adult literacy on the 5 planets that spend the most on primary students? + sp-7.svg||79.3
item_id: What is the average adult literacy on the 5 planets that spend the most on primary students? + sp-7.svg
reasoning_trace: Averaging the top-5 spenders' literacy gives 82.9, with low-literacy Helicon (~25) already included. A participant who misidentifies the top-5 spender set — for example including an additional mid-spending, low-literacy planet like Bolovax (~53) or Glazzon (~43) in place of a high-literacy high spender, because the x-positions of mid-range points are hard to rank precisely — pulls the mean below the true value toward 79.3. Alternatively, someone who correctly picks the five planets but visually anchors the average near the vertical middle of the point spread (between ~25 and ~90) lands below the true mean. Either way the direction of error indicates over-weighting the low-literacy points in the selected set.
misconception: Misranks similar x-positions when selecting the top-k points, swapping in a lower-valued point and biasing the aggregate downward.

key: What was the unemployment rate for Indiana (IN) in 2015? + item55.png||2.3% - 3.4%
item_id: What was the unemployment rate for Indiana (IN) in 2015? + item55.png
reasoning_trace: On the choropleth, Indiana is drawn in a light blue and sits directly between much darker neighbors (Illinois to the west, Ohio/Michigan around it). Simultaneous-contrast makes IN's fill look even lighter than it is, and when a participant carries that perceived shade to the legend they match it to the second-lightest swatch, whose label reads 2.3%-3.4%. Nearly half of participants chose this, showing a systematic perceptual pull rather than guessing. The correct answer (4.0%-5.0%) is not one of the legend's printed bin edges, so answering correctly requires resisting the direct swatch-label match; most readers instead trust their contrast-distorted shade match.
misconception: Judges a region's shade relative to its darker neighbors, so simultaneous contrast makes the region look lighter and match a lower legend bin.
short_label: Contrast with dark neighbors lightens shade

key: What was the unemployment rate for Indiana (IN) in 2015? + item55.png||3.4% - 4.6%
item_id: What was the unemployment rate for Indiana (IN) in 2015? + item55.png
reasoning_trace: Indiana's true 2015 rate falls in the 4.0%-5.0% option, but its fill on the map corresponds to the legend's middle shades. A participant carefully matching IN's color to the legend swatches lands on the 3.4%-4.6% swatch — a defensible one-step-light reading of a subtle color ramp with seven very similar blues. The legend labels bin edges rather than the exact value, and these readers pick the printed legend interval their shade match suggests instead of reasoning that the true value could span two bins (4.0-5.0 overlaps the 3.4-4.6 and 4.6-5.7 bins). Their relatively high ability (~0.58) supports this being a near-miss shade discrimination on adjacent legend steps.
misconception: Cannot reliably discriminate adjacent steps on a sequential color ramp, matching a region to the neighboring lighter legend bin.

key: What was the unemployment rate for Indiana (IN) in 2015? + item55.png||1.1% - 2.3%
item_id: What was the unemployment rate for Indiana (IN) in 2015? + item55.png
reasoning_trace: Indiana appears as one of the lighter states in its immediate neighborhood, boxed in by dark Illinois, Ohio, and Michigan. A participant who reads shade ordinally — 'IN is among the lightest states I can see here, so it must be in the lightest bins' — jumps to the lightest labeled interval, 1.1%-2.3%. This is the same contrast-driven lightness error as the 2.3%-3.4% choosers, taken one step further: the local comparison with dark neighbors substitutes entirely for a careful match against the legend swatches. The relatively high ability of these choosers (~0.64) suggests confident relative-shade reasoning applied where an absolute legend lookup was needed.
misconception: Infers a region's value from its lightness relative to nearby regions instead of matching against the absolute legend scale.

key: Which of the following is true about the residents in towns X and Y? + N11.png||There is a negative relationship between sleep quality score and average weekly hours spent outdoors for town X.
item_id: Which of the following is true about the residents in towns X and Y? + N11.png
wrong_answer: There is a negative relationship between sleep quality score and average weekly hours spent outdoors for town X.
reasoning_trace: Town X's dark-blue points span roughly 1-6.5 hours with sleep scores scattered from about 1 to 7.3 and only a weak upward drift; within X there is no negative trend. But several of X's highest scores (5.5-6.5) occur at the far left near 1-2 hours, while a handful of low scores near 3 sit at the right edge of X's range around 6 hours. A participant who judges association by connecting a few salient extreme points — top-left highs to bottom-right lows — perceives a downhill pattern and declares a negative relationship for X. This is judging correlation from extreme anchor points rather than the full point cloud, which here is noisy but mildly positive. The low mean ability of these choosers (~0.46) fits this shortcut.
misconception: Judges the direction of association from a few salient extreme points instead of the overall point cloud.

key: Which of the following is true about the residents in towns X and Y? + N11.png||Most residents in town X spend more than 6 hours outdoors every week.
item_id: Which of the following is true about the residents in towns X and Y? + N11.png
wrong_answer: Most residents in town X spend more than 6 hours outdoors every week.
reasoning_trace: The scatterplot distinguishes towns only by color: X is dark navy (concentrated between ~1 and ~6.5 hours) and Y is light green (mostly 5-12 hours). The full combined cloud clearly extends past 6 hours, and many points to the right of 6 exist — but they are nearly all green Y points. A participant who does not carefully apply the color legend, or who evaluates the claim against the whole point cloud rather than the X subset, sees plenty of residents beyond 6 hours and endorses the statement. The navy/green distinction also strains encoding: near the overlap region (5-6.5 hours) the intermingled colors make it easy to attribute green points to X.
misconception: Evaluates a claim about one color-coded subgroup against the entire point cloud, ignoring or misapplying the color legend.
short_label: Ignores color legend, judges whole cloud

key: Which of the following is true about the residents in towns X and Y? + N11.png||None of the above.
item_id: Which of the following is true about the residents in towns X and Y? + N11.png
reasoning_trace: Town Y's green points clearly rise from around scores of 3-5 at 5-7 hours to 7-11 at 9-12 hours, a genuine positive relationship, so 'None of the above' is wrong. The choosers here had the highest mean ability (~0.69) in this item, which suggests test-savvy participants who — knowing CALVI-style items often contain trick statements — rejected each option with excess skepticism: X's trend is not negative (true), 'most X > 6 hours' is false (true), and then they discounted Y's positive trend as well, perhaps because Y's cloud is wide and noisy or because they suspected every offered statement was a trap. This is over-applied skepticism: treating a real, visible pattern as unsupported.
misconception: Over-applies skepticism learned from misleading-chart items, rejecting a genuinely supported statement as a trap.

key: Do U.S. states have a more similar number of sunny days in the summer or in the winter? + T1.png||Summer
item_id: Do U.S. states have a more similar number of sunny days in the summer or in the winter? + T1.png
reasoning_trace: In the summer map every state is filled with the identical dark red 'High (10+)' color, while the winter map shows three different shades. A participant reads uniform color as uniform data: 'all states are the same in summer, so they are most similar in summer.' But the summer bin is top-coded — '10+' collapses everything from 10 to any large number into one category, so states could differ wildly (say 12 vs 300 sunny days) and still share the color; similarity cannot actually be inferred. Over 76% chose Summer, showing how compelling the uniform-color cue is. The error is treating a coarse, open-ended legend bin as if it certified equal underlying values.
misconception: Treats identical color-bin membership as evidence the underlying values are similar, ignoring that a coarse or top-coded bin can hide large differences.
short_label: Same bin read as same value

key: Do U.S. states have a more similar number of sunny days in the summer or in the winter? + T1.png||Winter
item_id: Do U.S. states have a more similar number of sunny days in the summer or in the winter? + T1.png
reasoning_trace: The winter map displays three distinct legend categories across states, so states visibly differ in winter — choosing Winter goes against the dominant visual cue that pulled most people to Summer. A likely route: a participant reasons that winter values are confined to a known, bounded range (all three bins fall within 0 to 10+, and most states sit in the two lower bins spanning only 0-9 days), whereas the summer '10+' bin is unbounded, so winter values seem numerically closer together. Others may simply have second-guessed the obvious uniform-summer reading and flipped to the alternative concrete season rather than the 'Cannot be inferred' option. With only 7 choosers and low mean ability (~0.46), this looks like partial insight (distrust of the summer map) resolving into the wrong concrete answer.
misconception: Recognizes a chart's dominant cue is unreliable but still commits to a concrete answer instead of concluding the data are insufficient.

key: True or False: GDP per capita for country Z grew faster from 2000 to 2003 than from 2005 to 2008. + T27.png||False
item_id: True or False: GDP per capita for country Z grew faster from 2000 to 2003 than from 2005 to 2008. + T27.png
reasoning_trace: The y-axis is deliberately non-linear: gridlines step 10K, 20K, 30K, then 31K, 32K, 33K, 35K, 37K, 40K at equal visual spacing, so a $10,000 gap and a $1,000 gap occupy the same height. From 2000 to 2003 GDP rose from 10K to nearly 30K (about +20K), but this huge growth is compressed into a shallow-looking segment; from 2005 to 2008 GDP rose only 31K to ~37.4K (+6.4K), yet the expanded upper axis renders it much steeper. A participant judging growth by visual slope, without checking the printed axis labels, sees the later period climbing faster and answers False. Nearly 74% fell for this, the signature error of trusting slope on a distorted axis.
misconception: Judges rate of change from visual slope, assuming the y-axis is linear, so unevenly spaced axis intervals distort the comparison.

key: True or False: GDP per capita for country Z grew faster from 2000 to 2003 than from 2005 to 2008. + T27.png||Cannot be inferred / Inadequate Information
item_id: True or False: GDP per capita for country Z grew faster from 2000 to 2003 than from 2005 to 2008. + T27.png
reasoning_trace: Every data point in both periods is plotted against labeled gridlines (10K through 40K), so the comparison is fully answerable by reading values: +~20K in 2000-2003 versus +~6.4K in 2005-2008. A participant who notices that the y-axis intervals are irregular may conclude the chart is broken or untrustworthy and that nothing can be inferred from it, rather than realizing the printed labels still permit exact value lookups. This is the flip side of the axis trick: detecting the manipulation but responding by discarding the chart wholesale instead of reading through the distortion. Only 4 participants did this, with modest ability (~0.47).
misconception: On detecting a distorted or manipulated axis, discards the chart as unreadable instead of using the printed labels to extract values.

key: When was the average price of a pound of coffee beans at minimum? + item36.png||June 2014
item_id: When was the average price of a pound of coffee beans at minimum? + item36.png
reasoning_trace: The area chart declines from ~$5.90 in early 2013 and features a dramatic, narrow V-shaped plunge at June 2014 down to about $4.67 — the most visually striking feature on the chart. The true minimum, however, is at the far right: the series ends by sliding to roughly $4.59 in December 2014, slightly below the June dip but without any salient notch shape. A participant scanning for 'the low point' locks onto the sharp June valley and stops searching, never comparing its depth against the quieter terminal decline. The two lows differ by well under 0.1 on a 4.4-6.2 axis, so the comparison requires deliberate gridline reading that the salient V discourages. About 35% made exactly this error.
misconception: Identifies the global minimum with the most visually salient dip and fails to compare it against quieter low regions, especially at the series end.
short_label: Salient dip mistaken for global minimum

key: When was the average price of a pound of coffee beans at minimum? + item36.png||April 2013
item_id: When was the average price of a pound of coffee beans at minimum? + item36.png
reasoning_trace: April 2013 sits just after the chart's global maximum (March 2013, ~$6.00) in the highest-price region of the whole series, so it cannot plausibly be the minimum for anyone actually reading price levels. The most likely routes to this answer: the participant inverted the task and looked for when price was at its extreme peak (April 2013 adjoins the salient March spike), or anchored on the small local notch where price dips from the March peak to the April/May plateau (~$5.67) — the first 'valley' encountered when scanning left to right. With only 6 choosers and low mean ability (~0.46), this looks like a mix of task inversion and grabbing the first local dip, closer to noise than to a single systematic misreading.
misconception: Answers extremum questions with the first local dip or peak encountered when scanning, or inverts minimum and maximum.
short_label: First local extremum or inverted task

key: Within each city, is there a positive relationship between salary and average daily working hours? + T39.png||Yes
item_id: Within each city, is there a positive relationship between salary and average daily working hours? + T39.png
reasoning_trace: The scatterplot pools residents of cities A and B into identical black points — nothing in the encoding identifies which point belongs to which city — and overlays a single prominent upward regression line with a confidence band. A participant sees the fitted line rising from ~$570 at 1 hour to ~$1,100 at 12 hours and answers Yes, transferring the pooled trend to 'each city.' But the question asks about the within-city relationship, which cannot be evaluated because city membership is not shown (and the two visible lobes hint the pooled trend may be a between-group artifact, i.e., Simpson's paradox). The 56% who answered Yes read the aggregate trend line as if it certified the relationship at every subgroup level.
misconception: Assumes a trend in pooled data holds within each subgroup, even when the subgroups are not identifiable in the chart.

key: Within each city, is there a positive relationship between salary and average daily working hours? + T39.png||No
item_id: Within each city, is there a positive relationship between salary and average daily working hours? + T39.png
reasoning_trace: The point cloud has two visible lobes: a mass of points at 1-6 hours containing both high salaries (~$1,000+) and very low ones, and a right-side mass at 6-12 hours that is similarly spread. A participant who mentally identifies these lobes as the two cities and inspects each one sees no clean upward pattern inside either lobe — the left lobe even looks vaguely downward — and answers No. This shows partial sophistication (resisting the overlaid pooled regression line, attending to subgroups) but overcommits: since the chart never actually labels which points belong to city A versus B, the within-city relationship cannot be determined at all. Guessing the cluster structure substitutes for the missing grouping encoding.
misconception: Infers subgroup membership from apparent clusters when the grouping variable is not encoded, then answers as if subgroups were known.

key: In San Francisco, as the weather gets warmer, there is generally more rain. + line.png||True
item_id: In San Francisco, as the weather gets warmer, there is generally more rain. + line.png
reasoning_trace: The line chart shows monthly rainfall peaking in winter (Dec 100, Jan 110) and collapsing to near zero across the summer months (Jun-Aug ~1 mm), so warmer months clearly have less rain and the statement is False. Answering requires an integration step the chart does not draw: the reader must supply the outside knowledge that summer is the warm season and then check summer's rainfall. A participant who instead consults their general world model — in most of the continental climate zones people know, warm seasons bring thunderstorms and more rain — endorses the statement without letting the plotted data override the prior. The chart is unambiguous, so the ~19% answering True reflects prior belief substituting for chart lookup rather than a perceptual failure.
misconception: Answers from prior world knowledge about the domain instead of checking the plotted data that contradicts it.

key: The metro system in Shanghai has more ridership than the metro system in Beijing. + item53.png||True
item_id: The metro system in Shanghai has more ridership than the metro system in Beijing. + item53.png
reasoning_trace: In the bubble chart, ridership is encoded by bubble area, and Beijing's bubble is visibly larger than Shanghai's, so the statement is False. However, Shanghai's bubble sits above Beijing's (longer system, ~560 vs ~530 km) and further right (more stations, ~370 vs ~325), so Shanghai dominates Beijing on both positional dimensions. A participant who forgets that ridership lives in the size channel — or who defaults to position as the primary carrier of 'more' — sees Shanghai higher and to the right and concludes it has more ridership. The two bubbles are also similar enough in area that a reader relying on a quick size impression, biased by Shanghai's dominant position, fails to register Beijing's larger area. This substitution of position for the size encoding drove ~27% to True.
misconception: Reads the asked-about variable from x/y position instead of the bubble-size channel that actually encodes it.

key: When did unemployment first go above 9.9 on planet Tun? + lg1-table-10.png||04/01/09
item_id: When did unemployment first go above 9.9 on planet Tun? + lg1-table-10.png
reasoning_trace: In the table, Tun's column first exceeds 9.9 in June 2810 (10.1); in April 2809 Tun is only 9.4. But scanning the April 2809 row, the adjacent columns Tanith (10.4) and Mandel (11.7) both cross above 9.9 for the first time right there. A participant who slips one column over while scanning down the tightly packed grid — or who scans row-wise for 'the first value above 9.9' without locking onto Tun's column — finds the April 2809 row and reports its date. A secondary route is misreading Tun's 9.4 as already 'above 9.9' by comparing only the leading digit region. The column-tracking slip is the more systematic account for the ~14% who chose this.
misconception: Loses column alignment when scanning a table, attributing a neighboring column's value to the target column.

key: Which season has more rain, the summer or the spring? + radial.png||More in the summer
item_id: Which season has more rain, the summer or the spring? + radial.png
reasoning_trace: On the radial chart spring's wedges (Mar 60, Apr 40, May 2) are large while summer's (Jun, Jul, Aug at ~1 mm each) are barely visible slivers at the center, so spring obviously has far more rain; even the printed values confirm it. Only 3 participants with very low mean ability (~0.30) chose summer, and there is no visual feature of this chart that systematically pulls a reader toward summer for this comparison. The most plausible accounts are non-visual: confusing which quadrant carries which season label (the labels sit at the outer corners, diagonally across from their wedges' centers), inverting the question, or simple guessing. Given the low count and low ability, this is best classified as noise rather than a systematic misconception.
misconception: No systematic misconception; answer consistent with guessing or momentarily confusing which quadrant belongs to which season label.

key: Approximately, what is the total number of visitors at amusement park B as a proportion of that at amusement park C from May to December? + T8.png||200%
item_id: Approximately, what is the total number of visitors at amusement park B as a proportion of that at amusement park C from May to December? + T8.png
reasoning_trace: The stacked area chart's y-axis is truncated at 25000 (with a small break glyph at the bottom). Park C is the bottom layer, so its true value runs from 0 to about 29500, but only the sliver from 25000 to 29500 is visible, making C's band look about 4500 tall. Having rejected all three, they select 'None of the above'. These choosers had the highest mean ability (0.65) - they reasoned carefully about every option but still applied the default bigger-is-more size convention, missing that the legend is inverted, which makes the first option true. The error is a single unchecked assumption propagating through otherwise sound elimination.
misconception: Verifies each option under the default mark-size convention and concludes none is true, without validating the legend's (inverted) size-to-value mapping.

key: Are there more households with exactly 1 car than households with exactly 2 cars? + T29.png||Yes
item_id: Are there more households with exactly 1 car than households with exactly 2 cars? + T29.png
reasoning_trace: The pie chart's printed labels say 1 Car = 55% and 2 Cars = 20%, but the drawn slice angles contradict these labels: the '1 Car' slice occupies roughly a quarter of the circle, visually similar to or smaller than the '2 Cars' slice. Because the labels and the geometry disagree, the chart is internally inconsistent and no reliable inference is possible - the intended correct answer. The 77% of participants answering 'Yes' read the numeric labels (55% > 20%) and answered directly, never checking the labels against the slice areas. They treat printed annotations as authoritative and do not notice the encoding conflict that invalidates the chart. This is the designed trap of this misleading item: trusting text over a contradictory visual encoding.
misconception: Trusts printed data labels without checking them against the visual encoding, failing to notice when labels and geometry contradict and make the chart unreliable.

key: Are there more households with exactly 1 car than households with exactly 2 cars? + T29.png||No
item_id: Are there more households with exactly 1 car than households with exactly 2 cars? + T29.png

Like the 'Yes' group, they resolve the label-versus-area conflict by committing to one channel - here the geometry - rather than recognizing that the contradiction itself means the question cannot be answered from this chart. Area judgments in pies are also imprecise, making the distorted slices persuasive. The failure is not noticing (or not acting on) the inconsistency between the two encodings.
misconception: Judges pie proportions from drawn slice areas even when they contradict the printed labels, instead of flagging the inconsistency as uninterpretable.

Taking the legend at face value, D obviously exceeds C, and 89% of participants answered 'Yes'. The trap is that a gray '0 mm average precipitation over 15 years' for Brazil is not a real value - gray here functions as missing/no-data, and the implausible bin values signal the map cannot support the comparison, which is why 'Cannot be inferred' is keyed correct. Participants map colors to legend numbers mechanically without asking whether a zero-precipitation Brazil is plausible or whether gray means 'no data'. The high mean ability of these choosers shows how strong the pull of literal legend reading is on this deceptive item.
misconception: Takes a legend category labeled '0' at face value as a true measured value rather than recognizing it may denote missing data, drawing comparisons the data cannot support.

Region C (South America) is salmon ('Very Low') while region A (the US) is tan ('Intermediate'). A participant judging by visual intensity sees C as darker/more saturated than A and concludes C has higher prevalence, when the legend actually assigns C the lowest category. This was the most common error (26%), showing how strongly readers default to the darker-means-more heuristic instead of verifying each color against the legend labels.
misconception: Assumes darker or more saturated map colors always encode higher values, instead of checking each color against the legend's category labels when the color ramp is not monotonic.

misconception: Applies an assumed (inverted) ordering to a color legend - e.g., lighter means more, or top of legend means lowest - rather than reading the actual label attached to each swatch.

misconception: Perceives a value difference between two regions filled with the same legend color, influenced by surrounding patches and region size when comparing colors across distant map areas.

The dominant error (44%, chosen even by higher-ability respondents) comes from comparing relative bar heights within each panel without noticing the different axis baselines, aided by the 'Crosicol helps!' headline.
misconception: Judges the size of an effect from the visual proportion between bars without checking whether the y-axis is truncated, so a cut baseline exaggerates the apparent difference.

key: True or False: Within each town, is there a negative relationship between average daily working hours and happiness score? + T38.png||True

But within Town A (purple, clustered at 1-6.5 hours) and within Town B (blue, 5.5-12 hours) the point clouds are essentially trendless; the negative slope arises only because Town B works more hours AND is less happy overall. Over half of participants answered True by reading the prominent fitted line as the answer: they applied the aggregate relationship to each subgroup. This is the classic ecological/Simpson's-paradox trap the chart is designed around - the drawn trend line invites transferring the pooled pattern to within-group structure.
misconception: Applies a pooled/aggregate trend line to subgroups, assuming the overall relationship holds within each group.

Participants choosing 'Cannot be inferred' likely felt that because only one pooled regression line is drawn and no per-town fit lines are provided, the within-town relationship cannot be judged. reasoning_trace: Hivehom's bar is the lowest at about 48, but Gallo's bar a few positions to the right is barely taller at about 49.5 — a difference of roughly one percent of the axis range. With 20 unsorted bars and slanted labels, discriminating which of two near-equal short bars is shorter is a fine perceptual judgment, and no gridline sits between them to help. A participant who spots the cluster of short bars but resolves the tiny height difference the wrong way, or traces the wrong slanted label, answers Gallo. Only 3 respondents made this error, consistent with a near-threshold visual discrimination slip.
misconception: Misjudges which of two nearly equal-height bars is the extreme when the difference is below easy visual discrimination.

key: Which group of 2 planets (either red, orange, green, purple, brown, or pink) has the biggest difference in life expectancy? + bg-2.svg||Titan/Anarres
item_id: Which group of 2 planets (either red, orange, green, purple, brown, or pink) has the biggest difference in life expectancy? + bg-2.svg
reasoning_trace: The correct green pair Tazenda (~71) and Garon (~55) has a gap of about 15 years, while the orange pair Titan (~82) and Anarres (~72) differs by about 10. Titan is the single tallest bar on the whole chart, so the orange pair is visually the most salient. A participant scanning for 'biggest difference' latches onto the pair containing the most extreme bar, reading the size of the tallest bar as a proxy for the size of the within-pair gap. Because all the bars start at 0 and top out between 55 and 82, the actual gaps live in a narrow band near the bar tops, where a 10-year and a 15-year difference are hard to discriminate, so the salient tall pair wins.
misconception: Judges the difference between two bars by the height or salience of the taller bar rather than by the gap between the two bar tops.
short_label: Tallest bar substitutes for largest gap

key: Which group of 2 planets (either red, orange, green, purple, brown, or pink) has the biggest difference in life expectancy? + bg-2.svg||Contraxia/Muscaria
item_id: Which group of 2 planets (either red, orange, green, purple, brown, or pink) has the biggest difference in life expectancy? + bg-2.svg
reasoning_trace: The chart shows 20 tall bars whose tops are all packed between roughly 55 and 82, so every pair comparison happens in a thin band at the top of the plot. The brown/pink Contraxia/Muscaria pair sits at the far right of the wide chart, well away from the y-axis labels, making its gap especially hard to estimate against the correct green pair's ~15-year gap. With only 5 choosers (~6%) of average ability and no strong visual pull toward this pair, the response pattern looks like participants who could not confidently rank several similar-looking moderate gaps and settled on one of the remaining color pairs. There is no systematic feature of the chart that would specifically produce this answer.
misconception: When several bar pairs have visually similar gaps far from the axis, the choice among them becomes effectively arbitrary.

key: Which group of 2 planets (either red, orange, green, purple, brown, or pink) has the biggest difference in life expectancy? + bg-2.svg||Pyrassis/Marglot
item_id: Which group of 2 planets (either red, orange, green, purple, brown, or pink) has the biggest difference in life expectancy? + bg-2.svg

A participant who chose this pair is responding to the overall height of the two bars — both near the top of the axis — rather than to the difference between them. This is the same substitution seen with Titan/Anarres taken to its extreme: 'biggest' gets attached to the bars themselves instead of to the gap. Only 3 low-count responses show this, but the pull is systematic toward tall, visually dominant pairs.
misconception: Interprets 'biggest difference between two bars' as 'the pair with the biggest (tallest) bars'.
short_label: Pair height mistaken for pair difference

key: Which group of 2 planets (either red, orange, green, purple, brown, or pink) has the biggest difference in life expectancy? + bg-2.svg||Tissa/Kithrup
item_id: Which group of 2 planets (either red, orange, green, purple, brown, or pink) has the biggest difference in life expectancy? + bg-2.svg
