Its within-pair gap is not notably large, and only 3 participants (~3.5%) of roughly average ability chose it. Nothing about the encoding — no extreme bar, no adjacency trap — systematically drives readers to this pair; it is most consistent with participants who found the six pairwise gap comparisons too effortful, gave up on precise comparison, and picked a pair that looked 'different enough'. This pattern is noise rather than a shared misconception.
misconception: Under high comparison load, readers abandon systematic pairwise gap comparison and pick a plausible-looking option.

key: In which season does each month have less rain than the month before? + bar.png||Summer
item_id: In which season does each month have less rain than the month before? + bar.png
reasoning_trace: In the chart, Summer's three bars (Jun, Jul, Aug) are all essentially 1 mm — the flattest, driest season, visually almost empty. Spring is the season where each month strictly drops from the previous one (Feb 75 to Mar 60 to Apr 40 to May 2). A participant answering Summer has replaced the question 'in which season does rain decrease month over month' with the simpler question 'which season has the least rain', because the near-zero summer bars are the most striking low-rain feature of the graph. They read the tiny flat bars as the season 'with less rain' rather than checking the month-to-month trend within the season. This is the classic substitution of a level judgment for a trend judgment.
misconception: Substitutes 'which region of the chart has the lowest values' for a question about month-to-month decrease within a group.
short_label: Lowest level mistaken for decreasing trend

key: In which season does each month have less rain than the month before? + bar.png||Fall
item_id: In which season does each month have less rain than the month before? + bar.png
reasoning_trace: Fall's bars go 10 (Sep), 25 (Oct), 55 (Nov) — each month has MORE rain than the month before, the exact mirror image of the required pattern. A participant choosing Fall correctly noticed that Fall is the season with a consistent monotonic month-to-month change, but reversed the direction of the comparison in the question, reading 'each month has less rain than the month before' as 'each month before has less rain than the current one'. The chart's within-season ordering makes Fall the only steadily rising season, so this reversed reading picks Fall uniquely. The error is in parsing the comparative, not in reading the bars.
misconception: Reverses the direction of a 'less than the previous' comparison, selecting a monotonically increasing series instead of a decreasing one.

key: In which season does each month have less rain than the month before? + bar.png||Winter
item_id: In which season does each month have less rain than the month before? + bar.png
reasoning_trace: Winter shows Dec 100, Jan 110, Feb 75: the season contains the chart's biggest absolute drop (110 to 75, a 35 mm fall from Jan to Feb) and the tallest bars overall. A participant who chose Winter saw that large salient decline and generalized it to the whole season without verifying the first step, where rain actually rises from Dec 100 to Jan 110. They verified the condition on part of the season and stopped once one big decrease matched the question. The magnitude of the Jan-to-Feb drop makes it visually dominant over Spring's steady but less dramatic decline.
misconception: Verifies a 'holds for every point' condition on only the most salient subset of points instead of checking all consecutive pairs.

key: What is the approximate average life expectancy on this group of planets? + bg-1.svg||73.0
item_id: What is the approximate average life expectancy on this group of planets? + bg-1.svg
reasoning_trace: On this chart most of the visually dominant bars top out between 72 and 82 (Wanda 74, Voreg 81, Ydoc 81, Zoon 81, Hekla 82, Xanth 74, Radole 74, Aka 79), while a substantial minority sit in the mid-50s to mid-60s (Debstam 54, Durla 56, Delassia 60, Calafia 61, Nexon 62, Arrarat 63, Vincetori 65). The true mean is about 63, but 40% of participants said 73. Their eye draws a mental average line through the tops of the tall bars, which dominate the display, and the shorter bars are underweighted because they are fewer and less salient. So the estimate lands at the typical height of the tall cluster rather than the value-weighted mean of all 20 bars.
misconception: Estimates the average of a bar chart by the typical height of the tallest, most salient bars, underweighting the shorter bars.

key: What is the approximate average life expectancy on this group of planets? + bg-1.svg||53.2
item_id: What is the approximate average life expectancy on this group of planets? + bg-1.svg
reasoning_trace: The shortest bars on the chart (Debstam ~54, Durla ~56) sit right at 53-56, and the answer 53.2 matches the height of that low cluster. A participant who chose 53.2 appears to have anchored on the minimum region of the chart — perhaps reasoning that the 'average' should be near the bottom of the visible range of bar tops, or overcorrecting for the intuition that averages are pulled down by low values. Since the true mean is about 63 and most bars are well above 60, landing at 53 requires giving the few short bars far more weight than the many tall ones. Roughly 12% of participants show this low-anchored estimate.
misconception: Anchors an average estimate on the lowest values in the display, overweighting the short bars.

key: What is the approximate average life expectancy on this group of planets? + bg-1.svg||43.3
item_id: What is the approximate average life expectancy on this group of planets? + bg-1.svg
reasoning_trace: No feature of the chart points to 43: every one of the 20 bars is above 50, so 43.3 is below the entire visible range of bar tops. A participant choosing it cannot have derived it from any reasonable visual aggregation of the bars; the answer is the lowest option and was picked by only 3 people (~3%). This is most consistent with guessing or with picking the smallest number out of uncertainty rather than with any systematic reading of the chart.
misconception: Answer below the entire data range reflects guessing rather than any visual estimate.

key: What was the average price of a pound of coffee beans in September 2013? + item35.png||$5.20
item_id: What was the average price of a pound of coffee beans in September 2013? + item35.png
reasoning_trace: The x-axis spans two years, Jan 2013 through Dec 2014, with 'Sep' appearing twice. In September 2013 the price is about $5.10, but in September 2014 the curve peaks locally at about $5.21. A participant who answered $5.20 almost certainly located the wrong 'Sep' tick — the 2014 one — where the value reads $5.2, matching the distractor exactly. On a long two-year axis where month labels repeat and year labels appear only under January, it is easy to index into the wrong year. The relatively high ability of these choosers fits a careful value read at the wrong x position.
misconception: On a multi-year time axis with repeating month labels, reads the value at the same month in the wrong year.
short_label: Wrong year on repeating month axis

key: What was the average price of a pound of coffee beans in September 2013? + item35.png||$5.00
item_id: What was the average price of a pound of coffee beans in September 2013? + item35.png
reasoning_trace: At Sep 2013 the area boundary sits just above the 5.0 gridline, at about 5.10, roughly halfway to the 5.2 line. A participant answering $5.00 snapped their reading down to the nearest labeled gridline below the curve instead of interpolating between the 5.0 and 5.2 gridlines. The curve in that region is also descending and hovering near 5.0-5.15 for several months, encouraging a 'it's about five dollars' rounding. This is an interpolation/rounding error at the correct x position rather than a misindexing of the axis.
misconception: Rounds a value to the nearest labeled gridline instead of interpolating between gridlines.

key: What was the average price of a pound of coffee beans in September 2013? + item35.png||$4.90
item_id: What was the average price of a pound of coffee beans in September 2013? + item35.png
reasoning_trace: There is no point near September 2013 where the curve reads $4.90; the price does not fall to ~4.9 until Dec 2013 (about 4.95) and later dips in 2014. Choosers of this option had the lowest mean ability (0.39) and made up only 6% of responses. Reaching 4.90 would require both misplacing September and misreading the height, or simply picking a low-sounding plausible price. The pattern is most consistent with low-ability participants guessing among close distractors rather than any single systematic misreading.
misconception: Among closely spaced numeric distractors, low-ability readers guess rather than extract a value.

key: Which of the following is true about the education level of residents in city Z? + N13.png||None of the above.
item_id: Which of the following is true about the education level of residents in city Z? + N13.png
reasoning_trace: The pie shows Bachelor's 41% and Graduate 25%, so 'Bachelor's degree or above' is 41+25 = 66%, making the first statement true. A participant choosing 'None of the above' evaluated that statement against the single Bachelor's slice: 41% is well under 60%, so they judged it false; the graduate-majority claim (25%) and the Associate-vs-high-school claim (12% vs 5%) are indeed false, leaving 'none'. The failure is not perceiving the slices — these choosers had the highest mean ability — but failing to aggregate the two qualifying slices demanded by the phrase 'or above'. The wording requires a mental sum across categories, and they instead matched the statement to one labeled slice.
misconception: Evaluates a cumulative category ('X or above') against the single named slice instead of summing all qualifying slices.

key: Which of the following is true about the education level of residents in city Z? + N13.png||There are fewer residents whose education level is Associate degree than those with a high school degree.
item_id: Which of the following is true about the education level of residents in city Z? + N13.png
wrong_answer: There are fewer residents whose education level is Associate degree than those with a high school degree.
reasoning_trace: In the pie, Associate degree is the yellow 12% slice and high school degree is the small red 5% slice, so the statement is false — Associate is larger. Both are thin wedges sitting adjacent at the top of the pie, rendered in the two least saturated colors, and their identity must be recovered from the legend on the right. A participant choosing this option most plausibly swapped which thin slice belonged to which label when tracing the legend colors back to the chart, or compared the wrong pair (e.g., red 5% vs purple 17% 'Below high school'). Having mismapped the slices, the statement reads as true. The error lives in the color-to-category lookup for small adjacent slices, not in the proportional judgment itself.
misconception: Mismaps legend colors to slices when small, similar categories are adjacent, comparing the wrong pair of segments.

key: Which of the following is true about the education level of residents in city Z? + N13.png||The majority of residents have a graduate degree.
item_id: Which of the following is true about the education level of residents in city Z? + N13.png
wrong_answer: The majority of residents have a graduate degree.
reasoning_trace: The Graduate slice is 25% — the prominent green wedge at the upper right, the second largest in the pie — but far from a majority. A participant endorsing this statement either treated a large, salient slice as 'the majority' without checking it against the 50% threshold, or read 'graduate degree' loosely as 'have graduated / have a degree', which would cover the Bachelor's 41% plus Graduate 25% and feel like most residents. Either way, 'majority' is being used as 'a big share' rather than 'more than half'. The visual prominence of the green slice at the top of the pie supports the overestimate.
misconception: Treats 'majority' as meaning a large or plurality share rather than strictly more than 50%.

key: Between 1980 and 1990, which disease had a higher increase in the percentage of people affected? + ggr_item12.png||Coliosis
item_id: Between 1980 and 1990, which disease had a higher increase in the percentage of people affected? + ggr_item12.png
reasoning_trace: Between 1980 and 1990 the solid Coliosis line rises from about 28% to 31% (+3 points) while the dashed Tiosis line rises from about 12% to 20% (+8 points), so Tiosis has the larger increase. But Coliosis sits above Tiosis across the whole chart. A participant answering Coliosis read the question as 'which disease is higher' and reported the line with the greater level in that interval rather than comparing the two slopes. The vertical position of the lines is far more immediately available than the change over a sub-interval, so level substitutes for change. This is the classic slope/level confusion on multi-line charts.
misconception: Confuses a line's vertical level with its rate of change, answering 'which is higher' when asked 'which increased more'.

key: Between 1980 and 1990, which disease had a higher increase in the percentage of people affected? + ggr_item12.png||Cant say
item_id: Between 1980 and 1990, which disease had a higher increase in the percentage of people affected? + ggr_item12.png
reasoning_trace: The chart has gridlines only every 10 percentage points and no data-point markers or value labels at 1980 and 1990, so extracting the exact increases (+3 vs +8) requires interpolating both lines at two unlabeled years. A participant answering 'Cant say' concluded that without printed values the comparison cannot be made, even though the visibly steeper dashed Tiosis line answers the question qualitatively. Only 3 low-ability participants chose this, consistent with readers who do not trust or cannot perform slope comparison by eye and default to claiming insufficient information.
misconception: Believes a comparison of changes cannot be made without exact labeled values, ignoring that relative slope answers it visually.

key: How many people have rated the taxi between 4.0 and 4.2? + item22.png||240
item_id: How many people have rated the taxi between 4.0 and 4.2? + item22.png
reasoning_trace: In the histogram the bar over the 4.0-4.2 interval has height about 153, while the next bar to the right, spanning 4.2-4.4, has height about 240 — exactly the distractor. A participant answering 240 read the height of the adjacent bin: on a histogram the bar sits between two tick labels, and it is easy to attach the bar to the tick at its right edge or to index one bin over when the question names an interval boundary shared by two bars. Since 4.2 appears in both the target and neighboring bin definitions, they measured the wrong bar. The height read itself was accurate; the bin selection was not.
misconception: Selects the adjacent histogram bin when an interval endpoint is shared between two bars.

key: How many people have rated the taxi between 4.0 and 4.2? + item22.png||145
item_id: How many people have rated the taxi between 4.0 and 4.2? + item22.png
reasoning_trace: The 4.0-4.2 bar tops out at 153, just above the halfway point between the 150 gridline and 155; gridlines are only every 50 units. A participant answering 145 identified the correct bar but judged its top to be slightly below the 150 gridline rather than slightly above it — a small vertical estimation error in a chart where 8 units corresponds to a couple of pixels. The distractors 145 and 153 are deliberately close, so any slight underestimate of the bar top selects 145. The low mean ability of these choosers fits imprecise height reading rather than a conceptual failure.
misconception: Misjudges a bar's height relative to a nearby gridline when distractors differ by less than the gridline spacing.

key: What is the education level of people in which the Democrats have the lowest approval rating? + item17.png||High School Graduate or Less
item_id: What is the education level of people in which the Democrats have the lowest approval rating? + item17.png
reasoning_trace: In the 100% stacked bars, the blue Democrat segment is largest for High School Graduate or Less (~61%) and smallest for College Graduate (~47%), so HS-or-less is actually where Democrats do best. Notably, HS-or-less is also where the red Republican segment is smallest (~36%). A participant choosing it either reversed the superlative — reporting where the Democrat segment is most extreme/salient rather than lowest — or performed the lookup on the wrong party's segment, finding the column where the red block is shortest. Because the blue segments all start at 0% and differ only at their tops (61, 51, 47, 53), while the red blocks hang from 100%, the red segment lengths are easier to compare and can hijack the judgment. Either way the answer is the exact opposite column from the correct one.
misconception: In a stacked bar comparison, reads the extreme of the wrong segment (or wrong direction), reporting where the other party's share is lowest.

key: What is the education level of people in which the Democrats have the lowest approval rating? + item17.png||Postgraduate study
item_id: What is the education level of people in which the Democrats have the lowest approval rating? + item17.png
reasoning_trace: The Democrat (blue) segments top out at about 61%, 51%, 47%, and 53% across the four education groups; Postgraduate (53%) is not the lowest — College Graduate (47%) is — but the two differ by only ~6 points at similar heights near the middle of the chart. Only 3 participants with the lowest mean ability (0.37) chose Postgraduate. Some may have expected highly educated voters to rate Democrats lowest, or simply failed to discriminate 47% from 53% at a glance, but with this count and ability profile the answer mostly reflects weak reading plus a rightmost-column guess rather than one clear systematic cause.
misconception: When segment tops differ by only a few percent, weak readers fail to discriminate them and answer from position or expectation.

key: Where is life expectancy roughly 66? + bg-11.svg||Tanjent
item_id: Where is life expectancy roughly 66? + bg-11.svg
reasoning_trace: Blasusarr's bar tops out at about 66.5, the correct answer; Tanjent's bar is about 63. The y-axis is labeled only every 10 units, so judging 66 requires interpolating within the unlabeled 60-70 band, and Tanjent, Hope, Calafia, and Blasusarr all top out within a few pixels of each other in that band. Tanjent is also the second bar from the left, immediately before Hope and one bar away from Blasusarr, so a reader scanning for 'a bar a bit above 60' can settle on the first candidate encountered. The choosers' relatively high ability (0.64) fits a careful reader making a small interpolation error between sparse gridlines, not a task misunderstanding.
misconception: Imprecise interpolation between widely spaced gridlines causes selection of a nearby bar a few units off the target value.

key: Where is life expectancy roughly 66? + bg-11.svg||Krylor
item_id: Where is life expectancy roughly 66? + bg-11.svg
reasoning_trace: Krylor, the last bar on the right, tops out at about 69 — within the same unlabeled 60-70 band as the correct Blasusarr (~66.5). With gridlines only at multiples of 10, distinguishing 66 from 69 requires fine interpolation, and Krylor's position at the chart edge next to the tall Konom bar (~76) can make it look shorter by contrast than it is. A participant who scanned from the right and found a bar 'roughly two-thirds up between 60 and 70' would accept Krylor without cross-checking closer candidates. This is the same small height-estimation error as the Tanjent choosers, landing on the other side of the target.
misconception: Accepts the first bar whose height falls loosely in the target band instead of comparing all near-target bars precisely.

key: Does expenditure per primary student seem to have a positive impact on adult literacy on planet Maarin? + sp-6.svg||Yes
item_id: Does expenditure per primary student seem to have a positive impact on adult literacy on planet Maarin? + sp-6.svg
reasoning_trace: Maarin sits at roughly (14, 29): among the highest expenditures on the chart but by far the lowest literacy, well below planets like Lystena (5, 95) that spend a third as much — so the answer is No. A participant answering Yes likely never isolated Maarin's point: they either evaluated the question against a general belief that education spending must improve literacy, or glanced at the scatter and assumed a positive association without noticing the plot actually shows no such trend. The question's framing ('seem to have a positive impact') invites confirming a prior rather than locating the labeled point at the bottom of the display. The below-average ability of these choosers fits answering from expectation instead of from the identified data point.
misconception: Answers a data-specific question from prior belief about the variables' relationship instead of locating the relevant point.

key: In the UK, the number of girls named 'Amelia' in 2014 was more than it was in 2013. + item44.png||True
item_id: In the UK, the number of girls named 'Amelia' in 2014 was more than it was in 2013. + item44.png
reasoning_trace: Amelia is the topmost band of the stacked area chart, so its value is the thickness of the light band, not the height of the top boundary. From 2013 to 2014 the top boundary of the chart rises slightly (about 13,600 to 13,900), but the band's thickness shrinks (roughly 5,900 down to 5,200) because the Isla and Olivia layers beneath it grow. Nearly three-quarters of participants answered True: they read the position of Amelia's upper edge — which is really the cumulative total of all three names — and saw it go up. This is the canonical stacked-area error of reading a stacked series by its top line rather than by band thickness.
misconception: Reads a stacked area series by the absolute position of its top boundary instead of by the band's thickness.
short_label: Stacked band read by top position

key: There is a negative linear relationship between the height and the weight of the 85 males. + item31.png||True
item_id: There is a negative linear relationship between the height and the weight of the 85 males. + item31.png
reasoning_trace: The scatterplot shows weight generally rising with height — points drift upward from about (163, 62) to (192, 102) — a moderate positive relationship, so the statement is false. Participants answering True saw a real linear association in the cloud but attached the wrong sign to it, either because they do not have a stable mapping between 'negative' and downward-sloping trends, or because the substantial vertical scatter and outliers (e.g., 124 kg at 175 cm) made them treat 'negative' as meaning 'weak/noisy'. The judgment that a relationship exists is correct; the direction label is what fails. This is a misunderstanding of correlation terminology rather than of the point positions.
misconception: Confuses the sign of a correlation, applying 'negative' to an upward-sloping or noisy relationship.

key: Which of the following states has the highest number of Lego owners? + N14.png||Cannot be inferred / inadequate information
item_id: Which of the following states has the highest number of Lego owners? + N14.png
reasoning_trace: The choropleth bins states into three classes: AZ is dark red High (100K+), NV is Intermediate (60K-90K), and TN is Low (0-50K), so AZ is unambiguously the highest of the three options. A participant choosing 'Cannot be inferred' reasoned that because the map shows only coarse ranges rather than exact counts, one cannot determine which state has 'the highest number'. That caution would be warranted if two options shared the top bin, but here the three named states fall in three different, non-overlapping ranges, so the ordinal comparison is fully determined. The high mean ability of these choosers (0.63) fits sophisticated readers over-applying skepticism about binned encodings on a test known for misleading items.
misconception: Assumes binned/classed encodings cannot support any comparison, even when the items fall in different non-overlapping bins.

key: Which planet has the lowest life expectancy? + bg-table-8.png||MMR
item_id: Which planet has the lowest life expectancy? + bg-table-8.png
reasoning_trace: The displayed table lists 20 fictional planets (Hala, Takron, Sirius, Methel...) with values, but the answer options participants saw are real-world country codes (MMR, RUS, USA...), so the options cannot be matched to the rows of the chart at all. Faced with this mismatch, participants could not literally look up the minimum (Methel 47.2 or Pacem 47.8, with the keyed answer Sirius also absent from the options), so they answered from what the labels mean in the real world. MMR (Myanmar) is a low-income country widely associated with poor health outcomes, so nearly half of participants - including relatively high-ability ones - selected it as the plausible 'lowest life expectancy' entry. The answer is driven by semantic prior knowledge about the labels rather than by any value shown in the table.
misconception: When answer options cannot be located in the chart, substitutes real-world prior knowledge about the labels for actually reading the encoded values.
short_label: Answers from prior knowledge, not data

key: Which planet has the lowest life expectancy? + bg-table-8.png||HUN
item_id: Which planet has the lowest life expectancy? + bg-table-8.png
reasoning_trace: The table shows fictional planet names, while the options are country codes, so a participant cannot find any option in the Planet column to compare values. With no way to ground the choice in the table, HUN (Hungary) is picked by only 3 people, which looks like near-random selection from a 20-item list, perhaps nudged by a vague sense that Eastern European countries have lower life expectancies. There is no value in the visible table that would systematically pull a reader toward HUN. The tiny count and mid-range ability of choosers are consistent with guessing under an unanswerable item.
misconception: When the chart cannot answer the question, picks an option essentially at random rather than flagging the mismatch.

key: Which planet has the lowest life expectancy? + bg-table-8.png||RUS
item_id: Which planet has the lowest life expectancy? + bg-table-8.png
reasoning_trace: Because the table's Planet column (Hala, Sirius, Methel...) shares no labels with the country-code options, participants had to fall back on what they know about the countries the codes denote. RUS (Russia) is stereotypically associated with depressed life expectancy (especially for men), making it a semantically attractive answer for 'lowest life expectancy' even though nothing in the table refers to it. Only 3 participants chose it, so it is a weakly-held prior-knowledge response rather than a chart-reading error. The chart's actual minimum (Methel, 47.2) plays no role in this choice.
misconception: Substitutes stereotyped world knowledge about label meanings for looking up values in the display.

key: Which planet has the lowest life expectancy? + bg-table-8.png||USA
item_id: Which planet has the lowest life expectancy? + bg-table-8.png
reasoning_trace: The options are country codes that never appear in the displayed planet table, so the item is unanswerable from the visualization. USA is by far the most familiar and visually salient code in the option list, and a small number of participants (3) appear to have defaulted to it, possibly recalling news narratives about declining US life expectancy. Notably these choosers had relatively high ability, consistent with a deliberate 'least unreasonable' selection under an impossible item rather than a systematic misreading of the table. Nothing in the table's values supports USA.
misconception: Defaults to the most familiar or salient option label when the chart does not contain the options.

key: In which season does each month have less rain than the month before? + line.png||Summer
item_id: In which season does each month have less rain than the month before? + line.png
reasoning_trace: The line chart shows rainfall falling steeply through Spring (Mar 60, Apr 40, May 2 - each month lower than the previous) and then sitting near zero across Summer (Jun, Jul, Aug all about 0-1 mm). A majority of participants answered Summer because Summer is where rainfall is visibly lowest - the flat stretch hugging the x-axis. They translated the question 'each month has less rain than the month before' into 'which season has the least rain', substituting an easier minimum-finding judgment for the required month-over-month decline check. In Summer the values are essentially flat, not consistently decreasing, so the answer fails the actual criterion, but it matches the low-value gestalt.
